Press Release:


Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa, the man who rose to power in a military coup, is in the hot seat. Free and fair elections could restore the political legitimacy of a government still isolated by the international community and suffering under the yoke of sanctions. Ahead of a much contested general election at the end of this month, Carte Blanche follows Mnangagwa on his campaign trail to Chinoyi, northern Zimbabwe, where he’s made bold promises to rebuild his country.

Script:


PRESIDENT MNANGAGWA


V/O: In November 2017 Emmerson Mnangagwa was sworn in as the third President of Zimababwe, following the resignation of Robert Mugabe. This former revolutionary and lawyer vowed to revitalize the economy and re-engage with the world. After 8 months in the hot seat, His Excellency, or HE as he’s called, is hard at work.

Devi: What has been the most challenging thing about being President?

HE: The most challenging thing in my view, is to make sure you are humble. There is nobody you must ignore. If you are able to accept views from people, you allow everybody to feel that they are accepted. That is very difficult, because with my background, I would not tolerate nonsense. But I’m now learning to be very humble and listen throughout. So, I’ve decided to be a listening President, and through that approach you find wisdom in corners where you don’t even expect it.

V/O: Thirty-seven years of Mugabe’s rule came to an end when the army seized control of the country. This soft coup was precipitated by the firing of Mnangagwa as Vice-President – a move widely seen as an attempt to further Grace Mugabe’s presidential ambitions.

President: I was very surprised that I was fired, because I didn’t even expect it. The letter of dismissal came to me about 5 o’clock in the evening when I was in my office, and by 7 o’clock I was already at home, and by 9 o’ clock I was on the run, because then I had received intelligence that certain elements in the system were after my life to eliminate me. So I left. But later on when I was in South Africa, I had opportunity to speak to my former boss, former President Mugabe. He said where are you, Emmerson? I said well, I’m in South Africa. What are you doing in South Africa? I said Mr. President you have forgotten. It’s not even a week since you have fired me. He says no, no, no, no- you should come back! I said I’m not safe, Your Excellency. No, no come back and stay with me at State House. No-one will touch you. So, I realized that even the issue of having fired me perhaps it was not a thing he was very conscious about.

V/O: It’s been reported the Mugabes have reached out to the opposition and may even vote for MDC leader Nelson Chamisa in the upcoming elections. This would mean turning his back on lifelong compatriots who marched with him on the road to liberation.

Link: Heroes Acre honors veterans who fought bravely for Zimbabwe’s independence. Here their legacy is set in stone. Robert Mugabe’s place in history is assured, but how that will be positioned remains to be seen.

Devi: What happens to the Mugabe’s now?

President: I have personally made sure that he has the best of retirement packages. No one on this continent has such a package. He is my icon and he is my founding father of this nation. Everything that is possible for me to do I will do to make him comfortable. And I’ve done so, and I’ve legislated so.

Link: The last time Carte Blanche was here in Zimbabwe we reported on the widespread farm invasions. Since the transition, the new President made headlines when he invited White farmers to return and farm their land. Could this new attitude take the country from begging bowl back to being the bread basket of Africa?

V/O: But farmers will not own the land again, they will be offered a 99-year lease.

President: All agricultural land in the country now belongs to the State. But it’s not the State which is going to develop it. It’s not the State which is going to make it productive, and we felt that a 99-year lease is long enough for somebody to invest and reap back their investment on that farm. And obviously the possibility of extension is of that 99-year lease is there.

Devi: Just about every Zimbabwean you speak to in South Africa says they want to come home. They feel it’s too soon to tell though, if they will have jobs or a place to live. What would you like to say to them?

President: I will say to them, not only Rome was not built un a day, even Jerusalem was not built in a day. We will build our country stone upon stone, brick upon brick and I would want my fellow citizens to come and put their individual on the collective stones to build our Zimbabwe together.

Devi: What is your vision for Zimbabwe? How do you see it turning around?

President: We must create an environment: the ease of doing business, the cost of doing business. We look at how those things can be done.

Devi: So, you are talking about the one stop shop where we reduce the amount of time it takes to start doing business in Zimbabwe?

President: It is true that in the past the registration of a company would take perhaps 70 to 90 days. Now I think. We are down to 4 to 5 days.

Devi: Forty-five?

President: No, down to 4 or 5 days.

Devi: I think we can learn some lessons from you.

President: After discussions with the President of Rwanda, he sent us a team running that sector. And they came here and spent some weeks with us here. I told him that there is now a danger that we may do better than him.

V/O: After the collapse of the economy, Zimbabwe has almost become a cashless society with over 80% of all commercial transactions being done on mobile phones.

Devi: How are we going to resolve the cash issue and currency issue moving forward?

President: It’s not a one-day wonder. We have a basket of currencies, and none of this basket of currencies do we have control over it. Currently we depend on the volumes of exports that we are making, and I’m happy that within less than 5 or 6 months our exports have jumped by 23%. I believe by September or October it may go up to 28% or 29% jump in terms of increase in exports. That is the only way we are having money in circulation.

V/O: There are now 133 political parties in Zimbabwe and the President has hit the campaign trail. But last month he narrowly escaped an assassination attempt while leaving the podium in Bulawayo.

Devi: Are you nervous in any way at all?

President: I’m passed nervousness in life. I’ve been in the military since the age of 19. I have seen many things happen. I also wonder why I’m still alive, but I thank God that I am.

V/O: But he too was accused of orchestrating political violence, while running Mugabe’s election campaign in 2008.

Devi: Given what has happened in previous elections, what assurance would you like to give the rest of the world that this election will be free and fair?

President: I’m saying to the people of Zimbabwe we must do things differently this time. Let us be open, we are an open society. We fought for democracy, let us see that democracy flourishing in our country. We must be transparent. So, I’ve said the doors are wide open for countries as well as international institutions who would want to observe our elections, come!

V/O: But it was while Mnangagwa was Minister of State Security that the Gukura/hundi happened, when 20 000 civilians were killed by the Zimbabwean Army.

Devi: A lot of bad things also did happen in Zimbabwe, where people lost their lives because of politics – the Matabeleland massacre – what would you like to say to them about moving into this new future?

President: No, we say let us learn from the past. The bad things that happened, we must abandon them. We don’t say we must forget about them, but we must say we made those mistakes, we must not repeat such mistakes again.

Link: As promised, Zimbabwe is having a general election at the end of July. The President is here in Chinhoyi having a heart to heart with voters, but one of the biggest differences between this rally and previous rallies is that Carte Blanche is here, and his main slogan is “the voice of the People, is the voice of God.”

President: When I was sitting in South Africa I saw on TV hundreds of thousands of people crying for change. I said “Mister President, I see what is happening: the demonstrations there. Between me and you, we have always said, and you taught me to say Emmerson, you must always respect the will of the people. In my view, the will of the people as you see it, is the will of God.” That is how it came about.

Devi: If you are successful in this election and you win it, how long do you plan on staying in power?

President: There’s no question of planning to stay in power. The Constitution already says how long a person stays in power. It’s 10 years, full stop.

Devi: First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa regularly makes unannounced visits to hospitals, children’s homes and prisons to understand their challenges.

President: All that she is doing is exposing these conditions in the country. And as a result of what she is doing she is pushing us as government to address those issues, but she is giving us more problems and more, more tasks to deal with. But we are only happy because you see, we have been blind to certain
disadvantaged groups in society. We did not know the conditions under which they are living, and every day she is unearthing these things. It is putting pressure on us to address those issues.

Devi: I’d love to meet the First Lady at some point, and I love the fact that she’s also putting you under pressure?

President: (Laughs) Ja, she’s putting me under pressure.

Devi: Your Excellency, in the event that ZANU-PF loses this election, will you accept the result?

President: If we lose these elections we will give the power to the political party which wins the election. This is democracy.
